name: Vietnamese (Southern)
variety: Southern Vietnamese, Saigon (Ho Chi Minh City)
sources: Thompson, Laurence C. (1965). A Vietnamese Grammar. University of Washington Press.
Brunelle, Marc (2009). Tone perception in Northern and Southern Vietnamese. Journal of Phonetics 37, 79-96.
Brunelle, Marc (2009). Northern and Southern Vietnamese tone coarticulation: a comparative case study. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 1.
Vũ, Thanh Phương (1982). Phonetic properties of Vietnamese tones across dialects. In David Bradley (ed.), Papers in South-East Asian Linguistics 8: Tonation. Pacific Linguistics.
Phạm, Ben & McLeod, Sharynne (2016). Consonants, vowels and tones across Vietnamese dialects. International Journal of Speech-Language Pathology 18(2).
Hoàng, Thị Châu (2004). Phương ngữ học tiếng Việt [Vietnamese dialectology]. Hà Nội: Nhà xuất bản Đại học Quốc gia Hà Nội.
Kirby, James P. (2011). Vietnamese (Hanoi Vietnamese). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 41(3), 381-392.

Đỗ, Thế Dũng, Trần, Thiên Hương & Boulakia, Georges (1998). Intonation in Vietnamese. In Daniel Hirst & Albert Di Cristo (eds.), Intonation Systems: A Survey of Twenty Languages. Cambridge University Press.
contrasts: five tones: hỏi and ngã are one tone; tones differ in pitch only, not in voice quality
retroflex ʈ ʂ (written tr, s) against palatal c and alveolar s (written ch, x) in careful speech; often merged in casual speech
implosive ɓ ɗ against voiceless unaspirated t, k and aspirated tʰ
long against short a and ɤ in closed syllables
final alveolars and velars are merged after most vowels: written n and t are said as ŋ and k
allophony: written v is [j] in everyday speech ([v] or [vj] in reading style and in careful speech), so v, d and gi are all [j]
written r varies between an approximant, a retroflex fricative, a tap and a trill [ɹ ~ ʐ ~ ɾ ~ r]; [ɣ] is a Mekong delta variant
written qu, and hu or ho before a vowel, are [w] (quả is [wa], huy is [wi])
final written n and t are velar [ŋ], [k̚] after all vowels except i and e, where they stay alveolar and the vowel is centralised (ăn is [ʔaŋ], mắt is [mak̚], tin is [tɨn])
final written nh and ch are alveolar [n], [t̚] with a centralised vowel (anh is [ʔăn], thích is [tʰɨt̚])
after rounded vowels final k and ŋ are labial-velar [k͡p̚], [ŋ͡m]
final p t k are unreleased
the centring diphthongs lose their second part before a final glide or m, p (rượu, nhiều, chuối, tiếp)
a syllable written with an initial vowel begins with a glottal stop
syllable_structure: (C)(w)V(C) plus tone; the coda is one of p t k m n ŋ or a glide j, w
phonotactics: syllables ending in a stop carry only the sắc or the nặng tone
the short vowels occur only in closed syllables

stress.rule: The last syllable of a phrase is the most prominent; grammatical words are weaker.
stress.cues: duration, intensity and fuller realisation of the tone contour

length.notes: Length is contrastive only for a against ă and ɤ against ɤ̆, in closed syllables.

intonation.declarative: lexical tones are kept; mild declination and a lower final tone
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by particles (không, hả, hông); register raised, last syllable higher
intonation.wh_question: question word in place; often a final particle (vậy, hả)
intonation.continuation: phrase-final lengthening and sustained pitch, then reset
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; emphasis widens the pitch range and lengthens the syllable

tone.confidence_notes: The five-tone system with merged hỏi and ngã and the absence of voice quality differences are well established (Brunelle 2009). The Chao digits are the conventional ones; sources differ by one step.

inventory.name: ngang, mid-high level; no tone mark
espeak_aliases: 7 (used on the last stressed syllable of a clause)
inventory.description: Mid to mid-high level, also written 44.

inventory.name: sắc, high rising; acute accent
inventory.description: Mid to high rising, also written 45; short and high in stop-final syllables.

inventory.name: hỏi and ngã (merged), low dipping-rising; hook above and tilde
espeak_aliases: 5 (ngã, which eSpeak NG keeps as a separate tone phoneme with a different contour)
inventory.description: Falls to low, then rises to mid or higher. Words written with hỏi and with ngã are said alike.
inventory.connected_speech: 21 or 212 inside a phrase, with a smaller rise

inventory.name: nặng, low dipping; dot below
inventory.description: Low fall with a slight final rise, also described as low level or low rising; not cut off by a glottal stop and clearly longer than Hanoi nặng. In stop-final syllables short and low.
inventory.duration: medium to long; short in stop-final syllables

sandhi: gradient tonal coarticulation only, carry-over stronger than anticipatory (Brunelle 2009)
tone.notes: Brunelle (2009) shows that Southern listeners identify tones by pitch alone, while Northern listeners also use voice quality; Southern tones have no breathy or glottalised members. No absolute F0 values are given here.

phonation: no voice quality differences between tones

problems: hỏi and ngã are kept as two tones with different contours (tone 4 a shallow dip high in the range, about 92 to 97 Hz; tone 5 a deep dip and high rise, about 93, 88, 104 Hz measured), where Saigon speech has one merged tone
hỏi lies in the upper part of the range and is nearly level, where the Southern tone is a low dipping rise
non-final ngang is a rise-fall (envelope i_risefall between pitch 20 and 35) instead of a level tone
no sentence intonation and no declination: CalcPitches_Tone() in src/libespeak-ng/intonation.c ignores the clause type, and a question gives the same audio as a statement
the tonal range is small: about 78 to 111 Hz with the voice setting 'pitch 82 118' (about 6 semitones, measured), and only sắc and ngã leave the band from 78 to 97 Hz
written r is the voiced velar fricative (phoneme Q), a delta variant, not the usual approximant or retroflex fricative
written s is the plain alveolar s, the same as x, and written tr is the same as ch; the retroflexes of careful Saigon speech are missing
written qu stays [kw] (quả), where Saigon has [w]

final n after i becomes a velar nasal with a central vowel (tin comes out as [təŋ]), and final nh mostly stays palatal (bánh, xinh; only plain anh gets n), where Saigon has an alveolar nasal in both cases
several vowels (i, E, a:, @, @:, O) are reset to a fixed length in ph_vietnam_sgn, which removes the coda-dependent durations of the Northern table
no tonal coarticulation, and a pause between all words ('words 1')
good: written v, d and gi all become a palatal fricative close to [j], and hu before a vowel becomes [w]
final written n and t become velars after most vowels, and au, ay have the Southern long-vowel forms
nặng has no glottal amplitude dip and is as long as the other tones, which suits the Southern tone
huyền is a plain low fall and sắc a wide rise

notes: The voice selects its rules with 'dictrules 2' and its sounds with the phoneme table vi-sgn, which inherits from vi. eSpeak NG tone numbers are the same as for Northern Vietnamese (1 ngang, 2 huyền, 3 sắc, 4 hỏi, 5 ngã, 6 nặng, 7 clause-final ngang) with different contours.
